title: Vector Addition and Subtraction: Analytical Methods
lead: The ruler and protractor of the graphical method give way here to sines, cosines, and the Pythagorean theorem. This section shows how to find the perpendicular components of a vector from its magnitude and direction, how to recover the magnitude and direction from the components, and how to add or subtract vectors by adding their components along each axis, which is more concise, accurate, and precise than any drawing can be.
objectives: Understand the rules of vector addition and subtraction using analytical methods.
Apply analytical methods to determine vertical and horizontal component vectors.
Apply analytical methods to determine the magnitude and direction of a resultant vector.
summary_html:
• The analytical method of vector addition and subtraction involves using the Pythagorean theorem and trigonometric identities to determine the magnitude and direction of a resultant vector.
  • The steps to add vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ using the analytical method are as follows:
    Step 1: Determine the coordinate system for the vectors. Then, determine the horizontal and vertical components of each vector using the equations $$\begin{aligned}\kAx &= \kA\cos\theta\\ \kBx &= \kB\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$ and $$\begin{aligned}\kAy &= \kA\sin\theta\\ \kBy &= \kB\sin\theta.\end{aligned}$$
    Step 2: Add the horizontal and vertical components of each vector to determine the components $\kRx$ and $\kRy$ of the resultant vector, $\mathbf{R}$: $$\kRx = \kAx + \kBx$$ and $$\kRy = \kAy + \kBy.$$
    Step 3: Use the Pythagorean theorem to determine the magnitude, $\kR$, of the resultant vector $\mathbf{R}$: $$\kR = \sqrt{\kRx^2 + \kRy^2}.$$
    Step 4: Use a trigonometric identity to determine the direction, $\theta$, of $\mathbf{R}$: $$\theta = \tan^{-1}(\kRy / \kRx).$$

exercises.prompt: Suppose you add two vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. What relative direction between them produces the resultant with the greatest magnitude? What is the maximum magnitude? What relative direction between them produces the resultant with the smallest magnitude? What is the minimum magnitude?

answer.solution: The resultant is greatest when the two vectors point in the same direction, since their components along that direction simply add, and its magnitude is then the sum of the magnitudes, $\kA + \kB$. The resultant is smallest when the two vectors point in opposite directions, since the components along that line cancel as far as they can, and its magnitude is then the difference of the magnitudes, $|\kA - \kB|$, which is zero only when the two magnitudes are equal. For any other angle between them the magnitude of the resultant lies between these two values.

exercises.prompt: Give an example of a nonzero vector that has a component of zero.

answer.solution: A displacement of 5 m straight east has an $x$-component of 5 m along an east–west axis and a $y$-component of zero along the north–south axis, since $\kAy = \kA\sin\theta$ and $\sin 0^\circ = 0$. Any vector that lies along one of the axes has a component of zero along the other, and its remaining component is as long as the vector itself.

exercises.prompt: Explain why a vector cannot have a component greater than its own magnitude.

answer.solution: The components are $\kAx = \kA\cos\theta$ and $\kAy = \kA\sin\theta$, and neither the cosine nor the sine of an angle can be greater than 1 in size, so each component is at most $\kA$. Put another way, the vector is the hypotenuse of the right triangle it forms with its components, and the hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle, so $\kA = \sqrt{\kAx^2 + \kAy^2}$ is at least as large as either leg.

exercises.prompt: If the vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are perpendicular, what is the component of $\mathbf{A}$ along the direction of $\mathbf{B}$? What is the component of $\mathbf{B}$ along the direction of $\mathbf{A}$?

answer.solution: Both components are zero. The component of a vector along a direction is its magnitude times the cosine of the angle between the vector and that direction, and $\cos 90^\circ = 0$. Choosing the $x$-axis along $\mathbf{A}$ and the $y$-axis along $\mathbf{B}$ makes this plain: each vector then lies along one axis and has no component along the other.

parts.hint: The displacement is 123 km at $45^\circ$ north of east, so the north component is $\kA\sin\theta$.
The east component is $\kA\cos\theta$, and at $45^\circ$ the two components are equal.

exercises.prompt: Solve the following problem using analytical techniques: Suppose you walk 18.0 m straight west and then 25.0 m straight north. How far are you from your starting point, and what is the compass direction of a line connecting your starting point to your final position? (If you represent the two legs of the walk as vector displacements $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, as in the figure, then this problem asks you to find their sum $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}$.) Note that you can also solve this graphically. Discuss why the analytical technique for solving this problem is potentially more accurate than the graphical technique.

answer.hint: With east as $x$ and north as $y$, the components of the resultant are $\kRx = -18.0\ \text{m}$ and $\kRy = 25.0\ \text{m}$; the magnitude comes from the Pythagorean theorem and the direction from the inverse tangent of the ratio of the legs.

figure.caption: The two displacements A and B add to give a total displacement R having magnitude R and direction θ.

exercises.prompt: Repeat problem 4 using analytical techniques, but reverse the order of the two legs of the walk and show that you get the same final result. (This problem shows that adding them in reverse order gives the same result—that is, $\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}$.) Discuss how taking another path to reach the same point might help to overcome an obstacle blocking your other path.

answer.hint: The components of the resultant are sums of the components of the legs, and a sum does not depend on the order of its terms, so $\kRx$ and $\kRy$ come out the same.

exercises.prompt: Do problem 4 again using analytical techniques and change the second leg of the walk to $25.0\ \text{m}$ straight south. (This is equivalent to subtracting $\mathbf{B}$ from $\mathbf{A}$—that is, finding $\mathbf{R}' = \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}$) (b) Repeat again, but now you first walk $25.0\ \text{m}$ north and then $18.0\ \text{m}$ east. (This is equivalent to subtract $\mathbf{A}$ from $\mathbf{B}$—that is, to find $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{C}$. Is that consistent with your result?)

parts.hint: The components of $-\mathbf{B}$ are the negatives of the components of $\mathbf{B}$, so the second leg contributes $-25.0\ \text{m}$ along $y$.
Both legs now have positive components, and the resultant points into the first quadrant, opposite to the resultant of part (a).

answer.solution: (a) $30.8\ \text{m}$, $54.2^\circ$ south of west (b) $30.8\ \text{m}$, $54.2^\circ$ north of east

exercises.prompt: You fly $32.0\ \text{km}$ in a straight line in still air in the direction $35.0^\circ$ south of west. (a) Find the distances you would have to fly straight south and then straight west to arrive at the same point. (This determination is equivalent to finding the components of the displacement along the south and west directions.) (b) Find the distances you would have to fly first in a direction $45.0^\circ$ south of west and then in a direction $45.0^\circ$ west of north. These are the components of the displacement along a different set of axes—one rotated $45^\circ$.

parts.hint: The displacement makes an angle of $10.0^\circ$ with the rotated axis, so its component along that axis is $32.0\ \text{km} \times \cos 10.0^\circ$.
The component along the other rotated axis is $32.0\ \text{km} \times \sin 10.0^\circ$.

answer.solution: (a) 18.4 km south, then 26.2 km west (b) 31.5 km at $45.0^\circ$ south of west, then 5.56 km at $45.0^\circ$ west of north

exercises.prompt: In an attempt to escape his island, Gilligan builds a raft and sets to sea. The wind shifts a great deal during the day, and he is blown along the following straight lines: $2.50\ \text{km}$ $45.0^\circ$ north of west; then $4.70\ \text{km}$ $60.0^\circ$ south of east; then $1.30\ \text{km}$ $25.0^\circ$ south of west; then $5.10\ \text{km}$ straight east; then $1.70\ \text{km}$ $5.00^\circ$ east of north; then $7.20\ \text{km}$ $55.0^\circ$ south of west; and finally $2.80\ \text{km}$ $10.0^\circ$ north of east. What is his final position relative to the island?

answer.hint: Take east as $x$ and north as $y$, find the components of each of the seven legs with the right signs, add the $x$-components and the $y$-components separately, and then find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.
